On a day of key injuries in the NFL, from Detroit and-or New England, some points of emphasis never change.
Recycling failed ideas won’t win back old friends for Israel
By Jonathan S. Tobin
(Nov. 16, 2026 / JNS) The U.S.-Israel relationship is at a crossroads. The future of an alliance that is vital to the Jewish state’s survival should be the subject of intense concern for Israelis and those who care about them. But the most important thing they should be currently doing is ignoring most of the advice they are receiving from the “experts” who are telling them how to fix it.
Such advice can be heard in both the United States and Israel. A feature published in The New York Times this past Sunday by David Halbfinger, its Jerusalem bureau chief, and an analysis in Yediot Achronot by prominent commentator Nadav Eyal that was also summarized in a lengthy and widely shared poston X, both put forward similar plans explaining how Israelis might win back the large number of Americans who seem to have turned their backs on them.

Bad ideas come back into fashion

The problem these pieces address is real and something Israel’s leaders must acknowledge. But their suggestions are not a product of contemporary thinking. Instead, they are rooted in nostalgia for a bygone past when the foreign-policy establishment could still pretend that their preferred solutions were considered realistic by those who paid attention to regional events. As such, rather than sage advice, they are a trap that will exacerbate Israel’s dilemma, and only make more bloodshed and war likely instead of peace.

Important in and of themselves, both articles reflect a consensus among the liberal elites that dominate the media, academia and cultural institutions in both countries.

Their prescription for Israelis is simple.

It starts with replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister with a new government, presumably led by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, Gen. Gadi Eisenkot, who has just received a mandate from Israeli President Isaac Herzog to attempt to do that. Halbfinger doesn’t specify who should be part of Eisenkot’s coalition, should the latter be able to form one out of the electoral stalemate produced by the Oct. 27 Israeli election for a new Knesset. By contrast, Eyal believes that such a government must include Arab parties that oppose Israel’s existence.

Both implore Eisenkot to prioritize employing draconian measures to end “settler violence” in Judea and Samaria. That is a narrative about the situation in the territories that is not merely false, but used to discredit Netanyahu, in addition to the hundreds of thousands of Jews who live there and the many more Israelis who support them.

The writers then go on to mandate a massive shift in Israeli security policies that would essentially return the country to the naive moment in 1993, when its government embraced the Oslo Accords. It was at that point that Israelis embarked on an attempt to trade “land for peace” that would end with the creation of a Palestinian Arab state alongside Israel, which would effectively end the conflict.

Forgetting 30 years of history

Both pieces sweep away the history of what followed—history that has shaped a broad consensus of Israeli opinion that rejects a return to the Oslo mindset.

That includes the suicide bombings and ensuing slaughter of more than 1,000 people in Israel during the years of the Second Intifada (2000-05), which was the Palestinian answer to the offer of Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and U.S. President Bill Clinton’s of such a state in the Gaza Strip, a share of Jerusalem and almost all of the so-called “West Bank.” It also means ignoring what happened when Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon withdrew every Israeli soldier, settler and settlement from Gaza in the summer of 2005 and how that led to the creation of a Hamas terror state there.

That epic blunder not only backfired. It set in motion the train of events that led to the events of Oct. 7, 2023, and the orgy of mass murder, torture, rape and kidnapping, as well as the subsequent war that produced the current impasse in the Middle East.

Israelis are urged to forget all of that. And they are told to turn a blind eye to the evidence that shows that the basic premise of “land for peace” was flawed—namely, that the Palestinians and those who seek to enable and encourage them abroad aren’t interested in two states or peace. What they want is Israel’s destruction—something that could only be achieved by the genocide of its population, for which the horror of Oct. 7 was merely the trailer.

In place of common-sense conclusions that Israelis, including many of those who voted for the “anyone-but-Bibi” coalition of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennet and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman, is an agenda of “change” that will require them to imagine a world in which they must stop thinking about defeating enemies like Iran, as well as its Hamas and Hezbollah terrorist proxies, and instead go back to trying to appease them.

The alternative, they are told, is to live in a world in which the Americans will abandon them. It is a world that leads to the end of Jewish sovereignty.

Moreover, they both demand that Israelis not delay abandoning a conviction that regards the conflict as a problem to be managed, rather than solved, because of the lack of a peace partner. They must, in both Halbfinger and Eyal’s versions, essentially surrender their security to the delusions that animate the left-wing J Street lobby. That advocates for overturning the will of the Israeli people as expressed in a quarter century of elections and instead imposes the foreign-policy establishment diktat of territorial surrender. This includes not merely Judea, Samaria and Jerusalem, but also the buffer zones Israel established in Southern Lebanon and Syria in order to prevent future terrorist attacks.

Declining support

Why would Israelis even consider such suicidal and irrational policies? They have already been proven not to advance peace. In fact, all movement in that direction has done is empower and encourage Arab and Islamist forces dedicated to Israel’s elimination and the slaughter of its people.

The answer of the “experts” is that many Americans think it’s a good idea. But that doesn’t make it correct.

It’s entirely true that the political problem Israel and its supporters are facing in the United States is serious—and just got worse with the election of Democratic Party majorities in the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate. They are likely to either attempt to place severe conditions on the alliance or try to blow it up altogether.

It’s also possible that two years from now, the next person elected president of the United States could be either deeply skeptical of the U.S.-Israel relationship or an open opponent of it. That could be the case whether the winner of the 2028 presidential election is either a Democrat or a Republican.

The reality is that support for Israel among Americans has declined since Oct. 7.

Polls had already demonstrated a rapid decline in backing for the Jewish state among Democrats in the decades before that awful day. The embrace of the toxic doctrines of critical race theory, intersectionality and settler-colonialism predisposed those on the left to accept the false notion that Jews and Israel are “white” oppressors, who are always in the wrong, and that Palestinians were “people of color,” who are always in the right, no matter what they did.

That set in motion the astonishing process by which the worst mass slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust was the excuse for an unprecedented surge of antisemitism. This was largely enabled by skewed coverage of the post-Oct. 7 war by journalists who had been indoctrinated in these doctrines, and thus willing to normalize and mainstream blood libels about Israel committing “genocide” in Gaza and being an “apartheid” state.

While Republicans still back Israel by large majorities, they are not unaffected by the same notions that dominate most of the American education system, as well as the media, popular culture and fine arts. That’s why younger Republicans fail to recognize that they, too, are being indoctrinated by anti-American and anti-Western ideas and therefore more likely to be less supportive of Israel than older ones.

Antisemitism isn’t caused by Israeli policies

The answer from the pro-Israel community to all this must involve a greater commitment of resources to efforts to counter the algorithms on social-media platforms that promote blood libels and support for independent media that reject these lies, like JNS.

And it must also be rooted in an acceptance of the fact that the antisemitism at the foundation of critiques of Israel’s efforts to defend itself against a genocidal foe cannot be wished away by changing the behavior of the Jewish state or the Jews as a whole. Jew-hatred is always about the Jew-haters.

In America, that’s why leftists peddle the myth that Israel and Jewish sovereignty are the purest expression of racism and settler-colonialism, and whose destruction will save the whole world. And it also explains why some on the far-right embrace myths about Israelis manipulating America to discard its interests as part of a conspiracy involving the Jeffrey Epstein sexual-misconduct scandal.

Neither left nor right is interested in the facts about the war on Israel and the Jews. What they care about is having a scapegoat on which to focus their fears about what troubles them most about the world or is the explanation for what scares them the most about it.

The myth that Halbfinger and Eyal are most interested in selling the Israelis and their allies is one in which the Jewish state’s problems are solely the product of mean-spirited right-wing attitudes promoted by Netanyahu and his coalition partners. They claim that fair-minded Americans who are shocked by the lies they accept about Israeli behavior in Gaza and the “West Bank” can be persuaded to preserve the alliance. Only if Israelis will reject a belief that they must defend their security and replace it with faith in the delusions about the willingness of the Palestinians and the Muslim world to live in peace with them that led a previous generation of leaders, like Shimon Peres and Barak, to believe in the fairy tale of a new Middle East that would resemble Belgium and the Netherlands.

Appeasement won’t win them back

But does anyone seriously believe that jailing the tiny minority of Jews who might be committing violence in Judea and Samaria in response to the daily toll of Arab terrorism there will fix Israel’s problems with those who believe in such nonsense?

Or that liberal Democrats who fear being primaried by radical Democratic Socialists because of insufficient hostility to Israel will be persuaded to reconstruct the long-gone bipartisan consensus in favor of the Jewish state? Even a government in Jerusalem that would try to revive a two-state solution that Palestinians have no interest in pursuing would ultimately be labeled an “obstacle” to peace by those who refuse to grant the objects of their sympathy any agency for their situation.

Or that those few Republicans, like apparently Vice President JD Vance, who think the antisemitic groyper vote will propel them to power would be happier with an Israeli government that puts its faith in policies designed by J Street? Would they embrace a weak Israel made vulnerable to its foes by concessions that will make it impossible to be the “America First” ally that is an asset rather than a burden to the United States?

There are no easy answers for Israelis as they confront a situation whereby Americans taught to believe that they are evil gain more power. They must instead become more self-reliant, as well as better-equipped to counter the lies spread about them.

What they cannot do is sacrifice their future survival by repeating the mistakes they made during the period when belief in Oslo—and the inevitability of land for peace and a two-state solution—dominated their politics.

Democrats will be more likely to welcome an Israeli prime minister not named Netanyahu to Washington. But in the long run, their caucuses and their base will not be satisfied by Israeli leaders, no matter who they are, if they aren’t willing to surrender their security or their state.

The reality Israelis understand

There is a reason why Eisenkot and his allies didn’t campaign for the policies embraced by J Street. Instead, they focused their efforts on ousting a prime minister who could be accused of being responsible for the Oct. 7 disaster that happened on his watch or on forcing the Haredim to serve in the Israeli military the way other Israeli Jews must. They did so because doing the bidding of those who claim that surrendering rational security policies will win them back American public opinion is rejected by the overwhelming majority of Israelis.

The Israeli people know that returning to efforts to trade land for peace, such as creating a Palestinian state in Judea and Samaria, and making even worse Oct. 7-style atrocities possible, is not so much ill-advised as it is insane. The fact that some misinformed or biased Americans disagree doesn’t change that they are right about this.

Attempting to win back U.S. support by listening to the advice of Halbfinger and Eyal will not just fail as politics. It is a formula for eviscerating the basic premise of the alliance, which rests on Israel’s ability to defend itself and be a vital pro-American force in a region filled with regimes that are neither democratic nor reliable friends of the United States. Moreover, the appeal to the common values rooted in the foundational beliefs of Western civilization that have long united the two peoples will not persuade those Americans, whether on the left or far right, who no longer embrace them.

The only alternative to this bad advice is for Israel—no matter who leads its government—to stay strong, reject suicidal concessions and do a better job of explaining itself to the world. Counseling to wait for a return to sanity in an American public square, where toxic forces have persuaded so many to buy into antisemitic blood libels and myths about Israel, isn’t satisfying to those who demand immediate solutions, even if they will make things worse.

Still, the pendulum of American politics never stops swinging. Those who assume that current intellectual fashions are permanent are always proven incorrect. And that includes those establishment figures who have always been wrong when it comes to their pet solutions to the conflict.

Until public opinion swings back in the direction of support for America’s sole democratic ally in the Middle East—the sole Jewish state on the planet—friends of Israel must continue to fight for the truth and refuse to be intimidated into surrender.

THE PARATROOPERS DROPPED INTO DISASTER

September 24, 1943. The Red Army launched 4,575 paratroopers behind German lines near the Dnieper. Many landed directly among German troops whose arrival Soviet intelligence had failed to detect.

Within hours, the airborne assault had collapsed. Some survivors would fight on for nearly two months.

The disaster was not caused by a single navigational error or an unexpectedly determined German defence. It was the result of an ambitious military plan overtaken by events, inadequate reconnaissance, unreliable transport arrangements and a command structure that committed its soldiers before the preparations necessary for success had been completed.

Yet what happened after the landing also deserves attention. The scattered paratroopers did not all perish in the initial fighting. Some reorganized in the forests of occupied Ukraine, disrupted German communications and eventually returned to Soviet lines after weeks of fighting behind the enemy.

Their story reveals both the remarkable endurance of Soviet soldiers and the terrible consequences of failures at higher levels of command.

The Strategic Opportunity

In September 1943, Germany's position on the Eastern Front was deteriorating rapidly. The German offensive at Kursk had failed in July, and the Soviet counteroffensives that followed had recaptured Oryol, Belgorod and Kharkiv. German formations were retreating westwards across Ukraine, abandoning territory in the hope of establishing a defensible position along the Dnieper River.

The river presented a formidable obstacle. Wide stretches of water, difficult approaches and high ground on the western bank offered defenders significant advantages. German commanders hoped the Dnieper would form the central obstacle in a broader defensive system often called the Eastern Wall.

The Soviet leadership was determined to prevent that line from becoming secure.

General Nikolai Vatutin's Voronezh Front advanced towards the Dnieper south of Kyiv, with Lieutenant-General Pavel Rybalko's 3rd Guards Tank Army leading the pursuit. By September 22, Soviet advance detachments had crossed the river near the Bukryn bend and secured several small footholds on its western bank.

These bridgeheads presented both an opportunity and a problem. Infantry could cross using small boats and improvised equipment, but establishing a sustainable offensive position required engineers, artillery, tanks, ammunition and supplies. The Germans could move reinforcements along roads on the western bank faster than Soviet forces could transport heavy equipment across the river.

The Soviet command therefore proposed an airborne operation to disrupt the German rear. Paratroopers would seize important terrain, interfere with reinforcements and help the ground armies transform their vulnerable footholds into a major bridgehead.

The concept was consistent with Soviet ideas of deep battle, which envisaged striking an enemy's communications and reserves while frontline forces attacked the main defensive position.

But doctrine alone could not overcome the practical requirements of an airborne operation.

An Ambitious Plan with Too Many Assumptions

The Soviets assembled a provisional airborne corps of approximately 10,000 men under Major-General Ivan Zatevakhin. It comprised the 1st, 3rd and 5th Guards Airborne Brigades, whose soldiers had been trained to land behind German lines and operate independently until ground forces could reach them.

The original plan included successive parachute landings, gliders carrying artillery, aerial reconnaissance, bombardment of German positions, air support after landing and continued deliveries of food and ammunition. Communications teams and artillery observers were supposed to accompany the airborne force, allowing its commanders to coordinate with Soviet armies on the eastern bank.

These arrangements suggest that the planners understood the requirements of such an operation. The failure lay in their inability to deliver them.

The front was moving rapidly, and railway shortages prevented troops and equipment from reaching their departure airfields according to schedule. Bad weather disrupted aircraft movements and aerial reconnaissance. By September 23, the Soviet command was forced to postpone the drop by twenty-four hours and alter the composition of the initial force.

Only the 3rd and 5th Guards Airborne Brigades would make the first landing. The 1st Brigade was held back, with the possibility of joining the operation later.

The revised orders reached subordinate commanders dangerously late.

Historian David Glantz records that brigade commanders received their final instructions roughly ninety minutes before loading, while company commanders had only fifteen minutes to explain their missions. Some platoon leaders were still briefing their soldiers aboard the aircraft.

Such delays mattered enormously. An airborne force could not simply land and begin fighting as an intact formation. Its men first had to locate their assembly areas, recover weapons, identify neighbouring units and determine where the enemy was positioned. These tasks were complicated even under favourable circumstances, and they became nearly impossible when soldiers had been given inadequate time to understand their objectives.

Worse still, the German army had been moving into the intended landing areas while the Soviets were completing their preparations.

The Enemy Was Already There

The German XXIV Panzer Corps had withdrawn towards the Dnieper and moved formations into defensive positions near Kaniv. By September 24, several of its divisions were occupying the area, while the 19th Panzer Division was moving towards the same sector from the Kyiv direction.

These movements transformed the situation on the western bank.

What had recently been a comparatively weakly defended area was becoming a concentration of experienced German infantry, armoured troops and supporting weapons. Instead of landing behind a thin defensive screen, the Soviet paratroopers were approaching positions occupied by forces already preparing to resist a Soviet breakthrough.

The Soviet command did not have an accurate picture of the enemy's deployment. Bad weather had prevented adequate aerial reconnaissance, and the speed of the German withdrawal meant that earlier intelligence was becoming obsolete.

The twenty-four-hour postponement, intended to address Soviet logistical difficulties, had also given German formations more time to occupy the intended landing zones.

This was the decisive intelligence failure. The entire operation depended upon assumptions about the enemy's location that were no longer valid, yet the assault proceeded.

September 24: The Landings Begin

The first aircraft carrying the 3rd Guards Airborne Brigade departed at approximately 18:30 on September 24. Aircraft carrying elements of the 5th Brigade followed later that evening.

Even before the paratroopers reached the river, the operation's transport arrangements began to unravel.

Aircraft had not assembled in sufficient numbers, pilots refused to carry the loads originally assigned to them, and inadequate refuelling facilities disrupted the carefully planned departure sequence. Soldiers and equipment were reassigned at short notice, with some men moving between aircraft in the hope of joining an earlier flight.

The consequences were substantial.

Of approximately 500 planned sorties, only 298 were flown. A total of 4,575 paratroopers reached the landing operation, accompanied by 660 light parachute bags containing ammunition and supplies. Another 2,017 men remained at the departure airfields.

The aircraft intended to deliver the 3rd Brigade's 45-millimetre antitank guns did not arrive in time. For soldiers who were about to encounter German armour, this omission would prove particularly serious.

The approaching aircraft then came under German antiaircraft fire.

Pilots manoeuvred to avoid the incoming fire, often flying at high speeds and altitudes that made accurate parachute drops extremely difficult. The absence of effective ground markers further complicated navigation.

The planned landing area measured approximately ten by fourteen kilometres. Instead, the troops were scattered across a region approximately thirty by ninety kilometres.

Some aircraft dropped their passengers east of the Dnieper among Soviet forces. Others released men into the river itself. Thirteen aircraft returned without dropping their passengers at all.

The most unfortunate soldiers descended directly into German positions.

Accounts from the 19th Panzer Division describe Soviet aircraft arriving over the village of Dubari just as German armoured and motorized troops were moving through the area. German soldiers opened fire on the descending paratroopers with rifles, machine guns and antiaircraft weapons.

Other Soviet groups landed among German supply columns, maintenance detachments and infantry formations. Some reached the ground only to discover that their designated assembly areas were already occupied.

The force had lost its concentration before the survivors could begin the mission for which they had trained.

From Airborne Assault to Scattered Resistance

The experience of a Soviet paratrooper landing near Kaniv varied enormously depending upon where his aircraft released him. A man who reached a wooded area with his equipment might have some chance of finding other survivors. A soldier who landed among German armoured vehicles or in an open field near a defensive position faced a very different prospect.

The original plan assumed that soldiers would gather into organized units, establish communications and move against assigned objectives. The scattered landings made those arrangements largely impossible.

Radios were lost, damaged or separated from the men responsible for operating them. Only five of the twenty-six radio sets carried by the force were initially functioning. Without communications, isolated groups could not determine where neighbouring units had landed, request reinforcements or coordinate with the Soviet armies attempting to cross the river.

German forces began systematic searches of the countryside on September 25. The white parachutes scattered across the landscape helped reveal the location of landings, while German patrols captured or destroyed much of the equipment dropped with the soldiers.

The results were devastating.

German accounts recorded hundreds of Soviet dead and prisoners within particular sectors during the first twenty-four hours. These figures describe local engagements rather than the complete losses of the operation, and German claims of having eliminated the airborne threat must be treated cautiously.

They nevertheless reveal how quickly the Soviet assault had deteriorated.

Within days, the Germans considered the immediate threat largely contained. The survivors were too dispersed to threaten the defensive line in the manner Soviet planners had intended.

For the Red Army, the mission of seizing and holding important terrain behind the river had become impossible. The soldiers still in German-held territory were now fighting primarily to survive, reassemble and recover whatever supplies they could find.

Between September 25 and October 5, Soviet records identified forty-three separate groups containing approximately 2,300 men from the original landing force. Other soldiers had been killed, captured or isolated, while some had joined partisan detachments.

The survivors were fighting a war without the organization their commanders had intended to provide.

The Forests Around Kaniv

The terrain of central Ukraine became one of the most important factors determining the fate of the scattered soldiers.

In the northern landing areas, more open countryside and substantial German defensive positions made concealment difficult. Small groups moved independently, avoiding patrols and attempting to reach safer ground.

Farther south, wooded terrain provided better opportunities to assemble. In the forests around Kaniv, Lieutenant-Colonel Pavel Sidorchuk, commander of the 5th Guards Airborne Brigade, began gathering soldiers from different units.

By October 5, Sidorchuk had assembled approximately 600 men. The following day, a radio crew joined his formation and succeeded in establishing contact with Soviet headquarters. This communication link eventually permitted aircraft to deliver ammunition and other supplies, allowing the growing force to conduct more organized operations.

Sidorchuk's command gradually developed into a substantial fighting formation. It included infantry battalions, reconnaissance personnel, engineers and other specialists recovered from the original landing force.

The men no longer attempted to carry out the September mission. Instead, they attacked German installations, interfered with communications and gathered intelligence for the advancing Soviet armies.

Their activities also brought them into contact with partisan formations operating in occupied Ukraine. These groups had their own experience of German security operations and the difficult conditions of warfare behind the front.

On October 19, Sidorchuk moved his men towards the Tagancha forest, where another group of survivors joined them. The force now numbered more than 1,000 soldiers.

Three days later, on October 22, they struck the railway between Korsun and Tagancha station and destroyed a train. They subsequently attacked German positions and supply installations around Buda-Vorobievska and Potashnya.

The Germans responded with attacks on the Soviet forest positions, inflicting losses and forcing Sidorchuk to withdraw farther south.

By late October, however, the surviving brigade had grown to approximately 1,200 men. It continued conducting raids and reconnaissance, while its communications with Soviet headquarters provided a means of directing useful intelligence towards the advancing armies.

This was a considerable achievement by troops who had been scattered, isolated and badly supplied for weeks.

It was not, however, a reversal of the original failure. The September operation had not secured its intended defensive lines, and German reinforcements had not been prevented from containing the Bukryn bridgeheads.

The surviving force had adapted to a disaster rather than fulfilled the mission that produced it.

November 13: Another Attempt to Help the River Crossing

By November, Soviet forces were preparing further crossings of the Dnieper near Cherkasy. Sidorchuk's brigade, still operating in the German rear, established contact with the Soviet 52nd Army and received new orders.

The paratroopers were to attack German positions around Lozovok, Sekirna and Svidovok, capturing the settlements and supporting a crossing by the 254th Rifle Division.

This time, the surviving airborne troops were not expected to secure an extensive region independently. Their task was narrower: attack German positions from behind at the same time that Soviet ground forces crossed the river.

During the early hours of November 13, the paratroopers advanced against the villages. Fighting developed around Svidovok, where German strongpoints were supported by tanks. Soviet troops used infantry weapons, antitank rifles and surprise to overcome parts of the German defence.

Other detachments captured positions near Lozovok and Sekirna.

Yet the operation again encountered a serious coordination failure. The 254th Rifle Division was unable to make its planned crossing during the night, leaving Sidorchuk's men exposed to German counterattacks.

German reinforcements, supported by additional tanks, attacked Svidovok and forced the paratroopers to withdraw into the forests rather than risk encirclement.

The immediate tactical operation had not unfolded as intended, but the Soviet ground offensive continued.

By November 15, elements of the 254th Rifle Division and 52nd Army had linked up with the airborne survivors. Sidorchuk's brigade remained in combat for almost another two weeks before being withdrawn to the rear.

For men who had originally expected to participate in a relatively brief assault followed by relief from advancing ground forces, their ordeal had lasted approximately two months.

What Did the Operation Actually Achieve?

The September airborne mission was intended to help Soviet forces enlarge their Dnieper bridgeheads by securing terrain behind the German defences and preventing reinforcements from reaching the river.

It did not accomplish those objectives.

The scattered landings prevented the troops from forming the planned defensive perimeter, communications failed, important equipment never reached the battlefield and the German army retained sufficient freedom of action to contain the Bukryn bridgeheads.

Some surviving paratroopers eventually carried out useful raids, destroyed supplies, gathered intelligence and assisted later Soviet river crossings. Those achievements deserve recognition, but they belonged to an improvised campaign conducted after the original operation had effectively collapsed.

Historian David Glantz estimated that more than 60 per cent of the airborne force never returned. The figure should not be interpreted as an exact number of men killed, because the surviving records encompass soldiers who died, were captured, disappeared or remained unaccounted for after dispersal.

The human cost was nevertheless enormous.

The episode also influenced Soviet military practice. The Dnieper landing became the last major operational parachute assault conducted by the Red Army during the Second World War. Airborne troops continued serving throughout the conflict, but Soviet commanders increasingly employed these formations in conventional ground operations rather than repeating large parachute drops behind German lines.

The Red Army ultimately achieved major victories in the wider Dnieper campaign. Kyiv was liberated on November 6, 1943, and Soviet forces established important footholds west of the river that enabled further offensives during the winter.

Yet those victories came through sustained operations involving infantry, armour, engineers, artillery and enormous logistical effort, not through the successful execution of the September parachute assault.

Courage Cannot Repair a Failed Plan

The disaster near the Dnieper illustrates an uncomfortable truth about military history.

A successful campaign can contain catastrophically mismanaged operations, and the courage demonstrated by individual soldiers can coexist with serious failures by the commanders responsible for employing them.

The Soviet airborne troops were not simply inexperienced soldiers who failed to perform their assigned duties. Many were trained men committed to an operation whose essential requirements had not been met. Their commanders lacked reliable information about German deployments, the aircraft schedule had collapsed, and the landing force did not possess adequate heavy weapons or communications.

The decision to proceed transformed those deficiencies into a battlefield disaster.

For the survivors, what followed was a struggle shaped less by doctrine than by the practical requirements of staying alive. They gathered scattered comrades, recovered supplies, fought German patrols and moved through forests that offered protection from an enemy with greater mobility and firepower.

Some eventually became part of a reorganized force capable of conducting substantial attacks. Others were never recovered.

Their story deserves attention not because the initial operation succeeded, but because it failed so badly, and because the men who survived continued fighting long after the plans developed for them had ceased to have any meaning.

The Soviet victory in the Battle of the Dnieper was real, as was its strategic importance to the defeat of Nazi Germany. But so too were the lives lost in an airborne operation whose planners had failed to account for the conditions their soldiers would confront.

The distinction matters. Remembering the achievement of the Red Army does not require excusing the decisions that needlessly increased its losses.

And remembering the paratroopers who fought their way through the forests of Ukraine requires more than celebrating their endurance. It requires asking why so many of them were placed in that position in the first place.

text:
I joined the (less than) 1% of women in the world who have finished a marathon 

This time last year I was overweight and not running at all. I went on a weight loss journey where I lost 50 pounds and fell in love with running in the process. Ive become more disciplined and I love fitness + nutrition. I trained alone 5 days a week for 6 months straight despite my other obligations and committed to sobriety for over a year now.

This marathon was an absolute dog fight for 90% of the race. Everything that could have possibly gone wrong absolutely did. I trained for speed but Im disappointed I never got to use it. My quads and left abductor locked up early on and I never fully recovered for the rest of the race. That never happened to me before so I was troubleshooting the pain and running at the same time but every time I picked up speed it locked back up and I had to stop for aid. I couldnt keep a pacer from all the stopping without being able to sprint back up. My pace alerts on my watch didnt work. My back was bleeding from my running vest being tight where my bra clip was in the wrong place. My headphones randomly died so I was left the with sound of my feet hitting the pavement and the struggle in my breathing for hours as it was 30 degrees and the wind overtook me on the endless rolling hills I was underprepared for. I made the executive decision that I wasnt willing to get injured which led to me finishing at double my usual pace + 2 extra hours on feet. I gave it my best but this is not the best I have to offer and that’s okay. This race taught me so many things I could have only learned through experience. After I recover Im excited to train harder now that I know what to do!

Huge thanks to the spectators who showed OUT with support throughout the city, thats what I’ll remember most about this day. I loved high fiving kids, dancing with DJ’s, and helping out other struggling runners. As a Charlotte native, it was full circle for me to be the first in my bloodline to achieve this in the same streets I grew up in. Thank you to my friends and family for all your encouragement and support!

The end of a thing is a better than the beginning and patience is better than pride
